title: Van Hollen tells podcast he is ‘kicking the tires’ on potential run for president
summary: A campaign spokesperson for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed Thursday that the two-term senator who has developed an increasingly high national profile is “kicking the tires” on a potential run in 2028 for the U.S. presidency.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters June 19, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters June 19, 2026

A campaign spokesperson for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed Thursday that the two-term senator who has developed an increasingly high national profile is “kicking the tires” on a potential run in 2028 for the U.S. presidency.

The confirmation comes after Van Hollen spoke Wednesday on the On NOTUS podcast, when he said that “dramatic change” is needed in the nation’s capital. He also criticized the Trump administration’s “stupid” decision to go to war with Iran, and continued his increasingly sharp rhetoric against the government of Israel under longtime Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

When asked about a visit last weekend to New Hampshire, a traditional early stomping grounds for would-be presidential candidates, Van Hollen said he was invited to an event hosted by the Chesire County Democrats. It was a fundraiser held Sunday where Van Hollen served as a keynote speaker. New Hampshire has long held the nation’s first presidential primary, after Iowa’s party caucuses, but Democrats are actively considering a change in the lineup for 2028.

“If you’re asking me whether I think Democrats need to shake things up, you bet I do. I visited New Hampshire, kind of kicking the tires a little bit,” Van Hollen said on the podcast. “It’s pretty clear that operating from within the confines of the halls of Congress is not a successful recipe for actually getting change. Too often, we are in a bubble.”

Van Hollen said it was his meeting with Kilmar Abrego Garcia in El Salvador last year that changed how he viewed the insider establishment in Washington.

In state races across Maryland, it’s all about Trump as primary looms

“This person’s constitutional due process rights were just shredded. If you violate his rights, [then] you put the rights of the rest at risk,” he said of Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident who was deported without a hearing and who is still fighting court battles on several fronts to keep from being deported again.

Jacob Rubashkin, deputy editor for Inside Elections, said it wasn’t surprising that Van Hollen is contemplating a run for president. He called Van Hollen “a very savvy politician.”

“I think it’s been clear over the last year and a half that he has been intentionally raising his profile,” Rubashkin said. “He’s an ambitious guy who has worked hard to burnish his progressive bona fides and his foreign policy bona fides. Going down to El Salvador was a very big moment for him.”

Rubashkin said Maryland is in a rare spot to have “two serious presidential contenders” in Van Hollen and Gov. Wes Moore (D), who continues to deny presidential ambitions despite rumblings otherwise.

Moore’s campaign spokesperson Carter Elliott IV referred a reporter Thursday to Moore’s previous statements on being focused on reelection this fall and on improving Maryland. When asked about Van Hollen considering a presidential run, Elliott said, “no comment.”

As for the slightly more than 27-minute podcast, several parts focused on foreign affairs because of Van Hollen’s seat on the Foreign Affairs Committee.

Van Hollen said a Democratic presidential candidate should “believe in a United States foreign policy,” but cannot apply one set of standards against China for human rights abuses, for example, while not applying the same standard to the Israeli government for “extending the illegal occupation” into Palestinian territory.

Van Hollen, who was elected to the Senate in November 2016 after seven terms in the House from Montgomery County, said senior officials who served under the Obama and Biden administrations should acknowledge “mistakes” when it comes to foreign policy.

“Any senior official who was responsible for those decisions, who doesn’t very openly and plainly acknowledge how wrong they were … then you should not have a role in any future Democratic administration,” he said. “People who do acknowledge their mistakes, in a genuine, authentic way and not just kind of a check the box, we should talk about them about the role they can play.”

— Maryland Matters intern Will Hammann contributed to this story.
